inline_content.text:
Boundary condition application is a critical aspect of the Finite Element Method (FEM), as it ensures that the problem's physical constraints are satisfied. Incorrect implementation can lead to non-physical solutions or solver failures. Essential and natural boundary conditions are treated differently in the weak form, with essential conditions being directly applied to the solution space, while natural conditions are enforced through the residual. The Galerkin method, a foundational approach in FEM, relies on the correct application of boundary conditions to ensure that the residual is orthogonal to the chosen basis functions, leading to a system of algebraic equations.

The Spectral Element Method (SEM) and curved elements are two distinct approaches used in the Finite Element Method (FEM) to model complex geometries. SEM utilizes high-degree piecewise polynomials as basis functions, leveraging orthogonal polynomials like Chebyshev or Lagrange polynomials over non-uniform nodes, to achieve high-order accuracy. In contrast, curved elements are specialized finite elements that allow for more accurate modeling of domains with curved boundaries by using higher-order polynomial shapes. This approach reduces discretization errors compared to straight-edged elements. The use of curved elements, particularly in weak Galerkin methods, enhances the flexibility of the solution space, making SEM and curved elements suitable for different types of problems, with SEM exceling in computational fluid dynamics and seismic wave modeling, and curved elements being critical for complex geometries.

children.title: Introduction and Scope of the Finite Element Method

inline_content.text: The Finite Element Method (FEM) is a powerful numerical technique for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). A foundational approach in FEM is the Galerkin method, introduced by Boris Galerkin, which involves approximating the solution of a problem by projecting it onto a finite-dimensional space of basis functions, ensuring that the residual of the differential equation is orthogonal to the chosen basis functions

. This method forms the theoretical basis for modern FEM formulations. Furthermore, FEM can be applied to complex geometries using curved elements, which allow for more accurate modeling of domains with curved boundaries by using higher-order polynomial shapes

.

The assembly and solution of the finite element equations are crucial steps in the Finite Element Method. The local element equations are assembled into a global system of algebraic equations, which is then solved using numerical methods such as direct solvers or iterative techniques. For limit analysis, optimization algorithms replace traditional solvers to compute collapse loads directly, as shown in the optimization problem

The Finite Element Method (FEM) has been extended to incorporate high-order and domain decomposition techniques to improve its accuracy and efficiency. High-order basis functions, such as those used in the Spectral Element Method (SEM), enable exponential error decay, reducing the number of degrees of freedom required for smooth solutions. This is particularly beneficial for high-frequency wave simulations. Furthermore, domain decomposition methods, such as the Additive Schwarz Method, allow for the division of the computational domain into subdomains, improving convergence for elliptic problems.
